Finance term: Gold Standard,Exchange Rate Regimes in the International Financial System
Definition: Before World War I, the world economy operated under the **gold standard**, a fixed exchange rate regime in which the currency of most countries was convertible directly into gold at fixed rates, so exchange rates between currencies were also fixed. American dollar bills, for example, could be turned in to the U.S. Treasury and exchanged for approximately \\(\\frac{1}{20}\\)ounce of gold. Likewise, the British Treasury would exchange \\(\\frac{1}{4}\\)ounce of gold for _L_I sterling. Because an American could convert $20 into 1 ounce of gold, which could be used to buy _L_+, the exchange rate between the pound and the dollar was effectively fixed at $5 to the pound. The fixed exchange rates under the gold standard had the important advantage of encouraging world trade by eliminating the uncertainty that occurs when exchange rates fluctuate.
As long as countries abided by the rules under the gold standard and kept their currencies backed by and convertible into gold, exchange rates remained fixed. However, adherence to the gold standard meant that a country had no control over its monetary policy, because its money supply was determined by gold flows between countries. Furthermore, monetary policy throughout the world was greatly influenced by the production of gold and gold discoveries. When gold production was low in the 1870s and 1880s, the money supply throughout the world grew slowly and did not keep pace with the growth of the world economy. The result was deflation (falling price levels). Gold discoveries in Alaska and South Africa in the 1890s greatly expanded gold production, causing money supplies to increase rapidly and price levels to rise (inflation) until World War I.

data.content:
Finance term: Stop-loss strategy
Definition: A stop-loss strategy is a hedging procedure applied by institutions that have written a call option with a strike price \(K\) to purchase one unit of stock. The strategy involves buying the stock when its price rises above \(K\) and selling it when it falls below \(K\). The goal is to maintain a naked position when the stock price is less than \(K\) and a covered position when it exceeds \(K\). This method is designed to ensure that by time \(T\), the institution will own the stock if the option closes in the money and will not own it if the option closes out of the money.

The initial cost of implementing the hedge is \(S_{0}\) if \(S_{0}>K\) and zero otherwise. The total cost \(Q\) of writing and hedging the option appears to equate to the option's initial intrinsic value:

\[
Q=\max(S_{0}-K,\;0) \tag{11}
\]

Assuming no transaction costs, this would suggest that the hedging procedure works efficiently. Moreover, it implies that the hedging cost is always less than the Black-Scholes-Merton price, creating an opportunity for riskless profit by writing options and hedging them.

However, there are two critical reasons why equation (11) is incorrect. First, cash flows for the hedger occur at different times and need to be discounted. Second, purchases and sales cannot be executed at the same price \(K\). In efficient markets, hedgers cannot predict whether the stock price will remain above or drop below \(K\) when it reaches that level. Therefore, actual purchases must occur at \(K+\epsilon\) and sales at \(K-\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\) is a small positive number. This means every buy and sell transaction incurs an additional cost of \(2\epsilon\).

In an effort to mitigate costs, hedgers may choose to monitor price movements more closely, thus reducing \(\epsilon\). However, as \(\epsilon\) approaches zero, the frequency of trades increases, leading to a trade-off between lower costs per transaction and higher overall trading volume. Consequently, as \(\epsilon\to 0\), the expected number of trades tends toward infinity.

While the stop-loss strategy may appear appealing, its effectiveness as a hedging mechanism is questionable, particularly for out-of-the-money options. If the stock price doesn't reach the strike price \(K\), hedging costs remain zero. Conversely, if the price fluctuates around \(K\), the strategy can become expensive. Monte Carlo simulations can evaluate the strategy's overall performance by sampling various stock price paths and reviewing the outcomes. The performance measure for hedging, shown in Table 19.1, is the ratio of the standard deviation of hedging costs to the Black-Scholes-Merton price. A robust hedging scheme should yield a measure close to zero; however, in this case, it remains above 0.7 regardless of how small \(\Delta t\) is, thereby indicating that the stop-loss strategy is not an effective hedging procedure.

\begin{tabular}{c|cccccc}
\hline
$\Delta t$ (weeks) & 5    & 4    & 2    & 1    & 0.5  & 0.25 \\ \hline
Hedge performance   & 0.98 & 0.93 & 0.83 & 0.79 & 0.77 & 0.76 \\

data.content:
Finance term: unsystematic,Portfolio risk
Definition: A systematic risk is one that influences a large number of assets, each to a greater or lesser extent. Because systematic risks have marketwide effects, they are sometimes called market risks. 
 An unsystematic risk is one that affects a single asset or a small group of assets. Because these risks are unique to individual companies or assets, they are sometimes called unique or asset-specific risks. We will use these terms interchangeably. 

 The distinction between a systematic risk and an unsystematic risk is never really as exact as we make it out to be. Even the most narrow and peculiar bit of news about a company ripples through the economy. This is true because every enterprise, no matter how tiny, is a part of the economy. It's like the tale of a kingdom that was lost because one horse lost a shoe. This is mostly hairsplitting, however. Some risks are clearly much more general than others. We'll see some evidence on this point in just a moment.

The distinction between the types of risk allows us to break down the surprise portion, \(U\), of the return on the Flyers stock into two parts. Earlier, we had the actual return broken down into its expected and surprise components:

\[R = \text{E}(R) + U\]

We now recognize that the total surprise component for Flyers, \(U\), has a systematic and an unsystematic component, so:

\[R = \text{E}(R) + \text{Systematic portion} + \text{Unsystematic portion}\]

Because it is traditional, we will use the Greek letter epsilon, **e**, to stand for the unsystematic portion. Because systematic risks are often called market risks, we will use the letter \(m\) to stand for the systematic part of the surprise. With these symbols, we can rewrite the formula for the total return:

\[R = \text{E}(R) + U=E(R)+m+\epsilon\]

The important thing about the way we have broken down the total surprise, \(U\), is that the unsystematic portion, **e**, is more or less unique to Flyers. For this reason, it is unrelated to the unsystematic portion of return on most other assets. To see why this is important, we need to return to the subject of portfolio risk.

Finance term: Risk-neutral valuation
Definition: Risk-neutral valuation is a fundamental principle in the pricing of derivatives, which operates under the assumption that investors are risk-neutral. In a risk-neutral world, investors do not require higher expected returns to compensate for increased risks, simplifying the pricing process. While our actual world is not risk-neutral—where increased risk typically demands higher returns—risk-neutral valuation allows accurate option pricing in both risk-neutral and real-world conditions. The valuation relies on the premise that risk preferences do not impact option prices when considered relative to the underlying stock prices.

Two key features define a risk-neutral world:
1. The expected return on an asset equals the risk-free rate.
2. The discount rate for expected payoffs on derivatives is also the risk-free rate.

In the context of risk-neutral valuation, the probability \\(p\\) reflects the chance of an upward movement in stock prices, with \\(1-p\\) indicating the probability of a downward movement. By assuming \\(u>e^{rT}\\), it follows that \\(0<p<1\\). The expected future payoff from the option is expressed as

\\[
pf_{u} + (1-p)f_{d}
\\]

The current value of the option can be derived from this expected future payoff discounted at the risk-free rate, formalized as

\\[
E(S_{T}) = pS_{0}u + (1-p)S_{0}d
\\]

Substituting the equation for \\(p\\) shows

\\[
E(S_{T}) = S_{0}e^{rT}
\\]

demonstrating that the stock price, on average, grows at the risk-free rate when \\(p\\) is the probability of an up movement. Thus, risk-neutral valuation holds true across various stock price evolutions and confirms that it is valid in all worlds, not just risk-neutral scenarios.

The practical approach to risk-neutral valuation involves determining the probabilities of different outcomes assuming a risk-neutral world, calculating the expected payoff from the derivative, and discounting it at the risk-free interest rate.

An extension of this framework concerning the market price of risk for a variable \\(\\theta\\) is defined as 

\\[
\\lambda = \\frac{\\mu - r}{\\sigma} \\tag{35.1}
\\]

with \\(r\\) as the risk-free rate, \\(\\mu\\) as the return dependent on \\(\\theta\\), and \\(\\sigma\\) as its volatility. The market price of risk \\(\\lambda\\) remains invariant regardless of the particular traded security employed.

For a real asset based on multiple variables \\(\\theta_{i}\\), with expected growth rates \\(m_{i}\\) and volatilities \\(s_{i}\\), the evolution can be described by 

\\[
d\\theta_{i}/\\theta_{i} = m_{i}dt + s_{i}dz_{i}
\\]

where \\(z_{i}\\) is a Wiener process. The market price of risk for each variable, \\(\\lambda_{i}\\), allows for the valuation of any asset depending on \\(\\theta_{i}\\) by:
1. Reducing the expected growth rate from \\(m_{i}\\) to \\(m_{i} - \\lambda_{i}s_{i}\\)
2. Discounting cash flows at the risk-free rate.

This framework effectively illustrates how risk-neutral valuation can be extended beyond direct applications to incorporate multiple underlying variables and maintain accurate asset pricing.

data.content:
Finance term: Friedman's Modern Quantity Theory of Money,Friedman's Modern Quantity Theory of Money
Definition: The theory of asset demand suggests that the demand for money is influenced by individual wealth and the expected returns of other assets compared to the expected return on money. Friedman formulated the demand for money as follows:

\[
\frac{M^{d}}{P} = f(Y_{p}, r_{b}-r_{m}, r_{e}-r_{m}, \pi^{e}-r_{m})
\]

where:
- \(\frac{M^{d}}{P}\) = demand for real money balances
- \(Y_{p}\) = Friedman's measure of wealth, known as permanent income
- \(r_{m}\) = expected return on money
- \(r_{b}\) = expected return on bonds
- \(r_{e}\) = expected return on equity (common stocks)
- \(\pi^{e}\) = expected inflation rate

The demand for money \(\frac{M^{d}}{P}\) is positively related to permanent income \(Y_{p}\) while negatively related to the terms \(r_{b}-r_{m}\), \(r_{e}-r_{m}\), and \(\pi^{e}-r_{m}\). 

Permanent income is the present discounted value of expected future income, representing a long-term average that minimizes fluctuations from short-run income changes. As such, the demand for money, influenced by permanent income, remains relatively stable despite business cycle fluctuations. 

Individuals can hold wealth in several forms, categorized by Friedman into three types of assets: bonds, equity, and goods. The demand for these assets relative to money is shaped by expected returns, reflected in the latter terms of the demand function. 

The expected return on money \(r_{m}\) is determined by two factors: the services provided by banks on deposits, such as check provision or bill payments, and interest payments on money balances. An increase in either of these factors generally raises the expected return on holding money.

The terms \(r_{b}-r_{m}\) and \(r_{e}-r_{m}\) compare the expected returns on bonds and equity, respectively, to money. As these terms increase, the relative attractiveness of money diminishes, leading to a decreased demand for money. Additionally, the term \(\pi^{e}-r_{m}\) compares the expected return on goods (driven by capital gains from price increases, reflecting inflation) to money. An increase in this term indicates that holding goods becomes more attractive compared to money, which also results in a decreased demand for money.

Overall, Friedman's model illustrates the dynamic interplay between wealth, asset returns, and the demand for money, emphasizing the stability of money demand during economic fluctuations while highlighting how relative returns on various assets influence money-holding behaviors.

Finance term: Traditional Interest-Rate Channels,Transmission Mechanisms of Monetary Policy
Definition: The traditional view of the monetary transmission mechanism illustrates how expansionary monetary policy impacts the economy through a schematic representation: 

Expansionary monetary policy \Rightarrow i_{t} \downarrow \Rightarrow l \uparrow \Rightarrow Y \uparrow.

An expansionary monetary policy results in a decrease in real interest rates (i_t, \downarrow), which lowers the cost of capital, thus increasing investment spending (l \uparrow) and boosting aggregate demand, leading to a rise in output (Y \uparrow). 

While Keynes highlighted the significance of businesses’ investment decisions, the exploration of monetary transmission channels recognized that consumer spending, particularly on housing and consumer durables (like cars and refrigerators), also qualifies as investment. Thus, the interest-rate channel applies to consumer expenditure as well.

A crucial aspect of this interest-rate transmission mechanism is its focus on real interest rates rather than nominal rates. Typically, the real long-term interest rate, rather than the short-term rate, has a more substantial effect on spending. When central banks adjust short-term nominal interest rates, it influences real interest rates across both short- and long-term bonds. This connection stems from the concept of _sticky prices_, indicating that aggregate price levels change slowly. Hence, a drop in short-term nominal rates from expansionary monetary policy also leads to lower short-term real interest rates. The expectations hypothesis of the term structure states that the long-term interest rate reflects an average of expected future short-term rates, meaning a persistent reduction in real short-term rates decreases the real long-term rate as well. Lower real interest rates then contribute to increases in business fixed investment, residential housing investment, inventory investment, and consumer durable expenditure, resulting in a rise in aggregate output.

The importance of real interest rates over nominal rates in driving spending highlights a mechanism through which monetary policy can stimulate the economy, even during deflationary periods. When nominal interest rates reach a zero floor, a commitment to future expansionary monetary policy can lead to higher expected price levels (P^{e} \uparrow) and expected inflation (\pi^{e} \uparrow). Consequently, this lowers the real interest rate (i_{r} = [i - \pi^{e}] \downarrow) despite nominal rates remaining fixed at zero, stimulating spending through the interest-rate channel:

Expansionary monetary policy \Rightarrow P^{e} \uparrow \Rightarrow \pi^{e} \uparrow \Rightarrow i_{r} \downarrow \Rightarrow I \uparrow \Rightarrow Y \uparrow.

This mechanism illustrates that monetary policy can remain effective even when nominal rates are constrained to zero. It also sheds light on monetarist views regarding the U.S. economy's ability to avoid a liquidity trap during the Great Depression, suggesting that expansionary monetary policy could have mitigated the sharp output decline experienced during that time.

Finance term: Stop-loss strategy
Definition: A stop-loss strategy is a hedging procedure applied by institutions that have written a call option with a strike price \(K\) to purchase one unit of stock. The strategy involves buying the stock when its price rises above \(K\) and selling it when it falls below \(K\). The goal is to maintain a naked position when the stock price is less than \(K\) and a covered position when it exceeds \(K\). This method is designed to ensure that by time \(T\), the institution will own the stock if the option closes in the money and will not own it if the option closes out of the money.

The initial cost of implementing the hedge is \(S_{0}\) if \(S_{0}>K\) and zero otherwise. The total cost \(Q\) of writing and hedging the option appears to equate to the option's initial intrinsic value:

\[
Q=\max(S_{0}-K,\;0) \tag{11}
\]

Assuming no transaction costs, this would suggest that the hedging procedure works efficiently. Moreover, it implies that the hedging cost is always less than the Black-Scholes-Merton price, creating an opportunity for riskless profit by writing options and hedging them.

However, there are two critical reasons why equation (11) is incorrect. First, cash flows for the hedger occur at different times and need to be discounted. Second, purchases and sales cannot be executed at the same price \(K\). In efficient markets, hedgers cannot predict whether the stock price will remain above or drop below \(K\) when it reaches that level. Therefore, actual purchases must occur at \(K+\epsilon\) and sales at \(K-\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\) is a small positive number. This means every buy and sell transaction incurs an additional cost of \(2\epsilon\).

In an effort to mitigate costs, hedgers may choose to monitor price movements more closely, thus reducing \(\epsilon\). However, as \(\epsilon\) approaches zero, the frequency of trades increases, leading to a trade-off between lower costs per transaction and higher overall trading volume. Consequently, as \(\epsilon\to 0\), the expected number of trades tends toward infinity.

While the stop-loss strategy may appear appealing, its effectiveness as a hedging mechanism is questionable, particularly for out-of-the-money options. If the stock price doesn't reach the strike price \(K\), hedging costs remain zero. Conversely, if the price fluctuates around \(K\), the strategy can become expensive. Monte Carlo simulations can evaluate the strategy's overall performance by sampling various stock price paths and reviewing the outcomes. The performance measure for hedging, shown in Table 19.1, is the ratio of the standard deviation of hedging costs to the Black-Scholes-Merton price. A robust hedging scheme should yield a measure close to zero; however, in this case, it remains above 0.7 regardless of how small \(\Delta t\) is, thereby indicating that the stop-loss strategy is not an effective hedging procedure.

The three-month OIS rate is the rate that can be swapped for the geometric average of the effective overnight federal funds rate.The higher 3-month LIBOR rate arises because there is more risk in making a single three-month loan to a creditworthy bank than a series of overnight loans to creditworthy banks.

data.content:
Finance term: OIS rate
Definition: An overnight indexed swap (OIS) is a swap where a fixed rate for a period (e.g., 1 month or 3 months) is exchanged for the geometric average of the overnight rates during the period. (The overnight rates are the average of the rates in brokered transactions as just described.) If, during a certain period, a bank borrows funds at the overnight rate (rolling the interest and principal forward each day), the interest rate it pays for the period is the geometric average of the overnight interest rates. Similarly, if it lends money at the overnight interest rate every day (rolling the interest and principal forward each day), the interest it earns for the period is also the geometric average of the overnight interest rates. An OIS therefore allows overnight borrowing or lending for a period to be swapped for borrowing or lending at a fixed rate for the period. The fixed rate in an OIS is referred to as the _OIS rate_. If the geometric average of daily rates for the period proves to be less than the fixed rate, there is a payment from the fixed-rate payer to the floating-rate payer at the end of the period; otherwise, there is a payment from the floating-rate payer to the fixed-rate payer at the end of the period.

This will lead to Bank A receiving the 3-month LIBOR rate and (assuming its creditworthiness remains acceptable to the overnight market) paying the 3-month overnight indexed swap rate. We might therefore expect the 3-month overnight indexed swap rate to equal the 3-month LIBOR rate. However, it is generally lower. This is because Bank A requires some compensation for the risk it is taking that Bank B will default on the 3-month LIBOR loan. The overnight lenders to Bank A bear much less risk than Bank A does when it lends to Bank B for 3 months. This is because they have the option of ceasing to lend to Bank A if Bank A's credit quality declines.

The OIS rate is a good proxy for the risk-free rate. The OIS rate is not totally risk-free, but it is very close to risk-free. Two sources of risk can be identified, both very small. The first is that there might be a default on an overnight loan between two financial institutions. The chance of this is very small because any hint of an imminent credit problem is likely to lead to a financial institution being excluded from the overnight market. The second is that there might be a default on the OIS swap itself.

However, the adjustment to an OIS swap rate to reflect default possibilities is generally very small (particularly if the OIS is collateralized).

Finance term: term structure of interest rates,determinants of,Bond yields
Definition: Short-term and long-term interest rates typically differ, with fluctuations that can either favor short-term or long-term rates. This difference is referred to as the **term structure of interest rates**, which indicates the _nominal_ interest rates on _default-free_, _pure discount_ bonds of varying maturities. The term structure reflects the pure time value of money without risk of default or ongoing payments.

The term structure can be upward sloping (when long-term rates exceed short-term rates), downward sloping (when short-term rates surpass long-term rates), or "humped" (initial increases in rates followed by declines). The most common modern shape is upward sloping, though the degree of steepness varies.

The shape of the term structure is determined by three primary components: the real rate of interest, the inflation premium, and the interest rate risk premium. The real rate of interest represents the compensation investors require for parting with their money, essentially the pure time value of money adjusted for inflation. It affects the overall level of interest rates, but does not shape the term structure.

The inflation premium influences the term structure significantly. Future inflation expectations lead investors to demand higher nominal rates, as inflation diminishes the value of future cash flows. When inflation is anticipated to rise, long-term rates usually exceed short-term rates, producing an upward-sloping term structure. Conversely, a downward-sloping structure often indicates expected falling inflation.

The inflation premium can be observed in U.S. Treasury yields. Comparing yields between Treasury Inflation Protection Securities (TIPS) and regular notes of similar maturities reveals the inflation premium, typically around 2 to 3 percent, representing investor compensation for inflation risks.

The third component, interest rate risk, pertains to the greater loss risk associated with longer-term bonds due to interest rate fluctuations. Consequently, investors demand a higher yield for bearing this risk, known as the **interest rate risk premium**, which increases with the term to maturity. As interest rate risk rises, the related premium increases at a decreasing rate.

In summary, the term structure embodies the interplay of the real rate of interest, the inflation premium, and the interest rate risk premium. An upward-sloping term structure may occur when inflation is expected to rise gradually while the interest rate risk premium increases; conversely, a downward slope may result from anticipated decreases in inflation that outweigh the risk premium. Additionally, while the real rate of interest may remain unchanged, expected future real rates can differ, leading to various shapes for the term structure, including the potential for a humped yield curve.

Finance term: Traditional Interest-Rate Channels,Transmission Mechanisms of Monetary Policy
Definition: The traditional view of the monetary transmission mechanism illustrates how expansionary monetary policy impacts the economy through a schematic representation: 

Expansionary monetary policy \Rightarrow i_{t} \downarrow \Rightarrow l \uparrow \Rightarrow Y \uparrow.

An expansionary monetary policy results in a decrease in real interest rates (i_t, \downarrow), which lowers the cost of capital, thus increasing investment spending (l \uparrow) and boosting aggregate demand, leading to a rise in output (Y \uparrow). 

While Keynes highlighted the significance of businesses’ investment decisions, the exploration of monetary transmission channels recognized that consumer spending, particularly on housing and consumer durables (like cars and refrigerators), also qualifies as investment. Thus, the interest-rate channel applies to consumer expenditure as well.

A crucial aspect of this interest-rate transmission mechanism is its focus on real interest rates rather than nominal rates. Typically, the real long-term interest rate, rather than the short-term rate, has a more substantial effect on spending. When central banks adjust short-term nominal interest rates, it influences real interest rates across both short- and long-term bonds. This connection stems from the concept of _sticky prices_, indicating that aggregate price levels change slowly. Hence, a drop in short-term nominal rates from expansionary monetary policy also leads to lower short-term real interest rates. The expectations hypothesis of the term structure states that the long-term interest rate reflects an average of expected future short-term rates, meaning a persistent reduction in real short-term rates decreases the real long-term rate as well. Lower real interest rates then contribute to increases in business fixed investment, residential housing investment, inventory investment, and consumer durable expenditure, resulting in a rise in aggregate output.

The importance of real interest rates over nominal rates in driving spending highlights a mechanism through which monetary policy can stimulate the economy, even during deflationary periods. When nominal interest rates reach a zero floor, a commitment to future expansionary monetary policy can lead to higher expected price levels (P^{e} \uparrow) and expected inflation (\pi^{e} \uparrow). Consequently, this lowers the real interest rate (i_{r} = [i - \pi^{e}] \downarrow) despite nominal rates remaining fixed at zero, stimulating spending through the interest-rate channel:

Expansionary monetary policy \Rightarrow P^{e} \uparrow \Rightarrow \pi^{e} \uparrow \Rightarrow i_{r} \downarrow \Rightarrow I \uparrow \Rightarrow Y \uparrow.

This mechanism illustrates that monetary policy can remain effective even when nominal rates are constrained to zero. It also sheds light on monetarist views regarding the U.S. economy's ability to avoid a liquidity trap during the Great Depression, suggesting that expansionary monetary policy could have mitigated the sharp output decline experienced during that time.

Finance term: rational expectations,The Theory of Rational Expectations
Definition: **Rational expectations** can be stated as follows: **Expectations will be identical to optimal forecasts** (_the best guess of the future_) **using all available information.
Formally, if X stands for the variable that is being forecast, X^{e} for the expectation of this variable, and X^{of} for the optimal forecast of X using all available information (the best guess possible of his driving time), the theory of rational expectations then simply says
X^{e}=X^{of}
That is, the expectation of X equals the optimal forecast using all available information.
Rational Behind the Theory: The incentives for equating expectations with optimal forecasts are especially strong in financial markets. In these markets, people with better forecasts of the future get rich. The application of the theory of rational expectations to financial markets (where it is called the **efficient market hypothesis** or the **theory of efficient capital markets**) is thus particularly useful.
Implications of the Theory are as follows:
1. _If there is a change in the way a variable moves, the way in which expectations of this variable are formed will change as well_.
2. _The forecast errors of expectations will, on average, be zero and cannot be predicted ahead of time_.

data.content:
Finance term: market value versus book value,Balance sheet
Definition: The values shown on the balance sheet for the firm's assets are _book values_ and generally are not what the assets are actually worth. Under **Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP)**, audited financial statements in the United States generally show assets at _historical cost_. In other words, assets are "carried on the books" at what the firm paid for them, no matter how long ago they were purchased or how much they are worth today.

For current assets, market value and book value might be somewhat similar because current assets are bought and converted into cash over a relatively short span of time. In other circumstances, the two values might differ quite a bit. Moreover, for fixed assets, it would be purely a coincidence if the actual market value of an asset (what the asset could be sold for) were equal to its book value. For example, a railroad might own enormous tracts of land purchased a century or more ago. What the railroad paid for that land could be hundreds or thousands of times less than what the land is worth today. The balance sheet would nonetheless show the historical cost.

The difference between market value and book value is important for understanding the impact of reported gains and losses. For example, to open the chapter, we discussed the huge charges against earnings taken by CBS. What actually happened is that these charges were the result of accounting rule changes that led to reductions in the book value of certain types of assets. However, a change in accounting rules all by itself has no effect on what the assets in question are really worth. Instead, the market value of an asset depends on things like its riskiness and cash flows, neither of which have anything to do with accounting.

The balance sheet is potentially useful to many different parties. A supplier might look at the size of accounts payable to see how promptly the firm pays its bills. A potential creditor would examine the liquidity and degree of financial leverage. Managers within the firm can track things like the amount of cash and the amount of inventory the firm keeps on hand. Uses such as these are discussed in more detail in Chapter 3.

Managers and investors will frequently be interested in knowing the value of the firm. This information is not on the balance sheet. The fact that balance sheet assets are listed at cost means that there is no necessary connection between the total assets shown and the value of the firm. Indeed, many of the most valuable assets a firm might have -- good management, a good reputation, talented employees--don't appear on the balance sheet at all.

Similarly, the shareholders' equity figure on the balance sheet and the true value of the stock need not be related. For example, in early 2006, the book value of IBM's equity was about $33 billion, while the market value was $129 billion. At the same time, Microsoft's book value was $44 billion, while the market value was $282 billion.

For financial managers, then, the accounting value of the stock is not an especially important concern; it is the market value that matters. Henceforth, whenever we speak of the value of an asset or the value of the firm, we will normally mean its _market value_. So, for example, when we say the goal of the financial manager is to increase the value of the stock, we mean the market value of the stock.

Finance term: Asset swap
Definition: In practice, the LIBOR/swap rate is often used as the risk-free benchmark when credit calculations are carried out. Asset swap spreads provide a useful direct estimate of the spread of bond yields over the LIBOR/swap curve.

To explain how asset swaps work, consider the situation where an asset swap spread for a particular bond is quoted as 150 basis points. There are three possible situations:

1. The bond sells for its par value of 100. The swap then involves one side (company A) paying the coupon on the bond and the other side (company B) paying LIBOR plus 150 basis points. Note that it is the promised coupons that are exchanged. The exchanges take place regardless of whether the bond defaults.
2. The bond sells below its par value, say, for 95. The swap is then structured so that, in addition to the coupons, company A pays $5 per $100 of notional principal at the outset. Company B pays LIBOR plus 150 basis points.
3. The underlying bond sells above par, say, for 108. The swap is then structured so that, in addition to LIBOR plus 150 basis points, company B makes a payment of $8 per $100 of principal at the outset. Company A pays the coupons.

The effect of all this is that the present value of the asset swap spread is the amount by which the price of the corporate bond is exceeded by the price of a similar risk-free bond where the risk-free rate is assumed to be given by the LIBOR/swap curve (see Problem 24.20). This result is useful for calculations such as those in Example 24.2.

\[R_{p} = .50 \times - 20\% + .50 \times 30\% = 5\%\]

Table 13.5 summarizes the remaining calculations. Notice that when a boom occurs, your portfolio will return 40 percent:

Finance term: market value versus book value,Balance sheet
Definition: The values shown on the balance sheet for the firm's assets are _book values_ and generally are not what the assets are actually worth. Under **Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP)**, audited financial statements in the United States generally show assets at _historical cost_. In other words, assets are "carried on the books" at what the firm paid for them, no matter how long ago they were purchased or how much they are worth today.

For current assets, market value and book value might be somewhat similar because current assets are bought and converted into cash over a relatively short span of time. In other circumstances, the two values might differ quite a bit. Moreover, for fixed assets, it would be purely a coincidence if the actual market value of an asset (what the asset could be sold for) were equal to its book value. For example, a railroad might own enormous tracts of land purchased a century or more ago. What the railroad paid for that land could be hundreds or thousands of times less than what the land is worth today. The balance sheet would nonetheless show the historical cost.

The difference between market value and book value is important for understanding the impact of reported gains and losses. For example, to open the chapter, we discussed the huge charges against earnings taken by CBS. What actually happened is that these charges were the result of accounting rule changes that led to reductions in the book value of certain types of assets. However, a change in accounting rules all by itself has no effect on what the assets in question are really worth. Instead, the market value of an asset depends on things like its riskiness and cash flows, neither of which have anything to do with accounting.

The balance sheet is potentially useful to many different parties. A supplier might look at the size of accounts payable to see how promptly the firm pays its bills. A potential creditor would examine the liquidity and degree of financial leverage. Managers within the firm can track things like the amount of cash and the amount of inventory the firm keeps on hand. Uses such as these are discussed in more detail in Chapter 3.

Managers and investors will frequently be interested in knowing the value of the firm. This information is not on the balance sheet. The fact that balance sheet assets are listed at cost means that there is no necessary connection between the total assets shown and the value of the firm. Indeed, many of the most valuable assets a firm might have -- good management, a good reputation, talented employees--don't appear on the balance sheet at all.

Similarly, the shareholders' equity figure on the balance sheet and the true value of the stock need not be related. For example, in early 2006, the book value of IBM's equity was about $33 billion, while the market value was $129 billion. At the same time, Microsoft's book value was $44 billion, while the market value was $282 billion.

For financial managers, then, the accounting value of the stock is not an especially important concern; it is the market value that matters. Henceforth, whenever we speak of the value of an asset or the value of the firm, we will normally mean its _market value_. So, for example, when we say the goal of the financial manager is to increase the value of the stock, we mean the market value of the stock.

Finance term: Zions Bancorp,Employee stock option
Definition: One way of valuing an employee stock option is to see what the market would pay for it. Cisco was the first to try this in 2006. It proposed selling options with the exact terms of its employee stock options to institutional investors. This approach was rejected by the SEC on the grounds that the range of investors bidding for the options was not wide enough.

Zions Bancorp has suggested an alternative approach. It proposed that securities providing payoffs mirroring those actually realized by its employees be sold. Suppose that the strike price for a particular grant to employees is $40 and it turns out that 1% of employees exercise after exactly 5 years when the stock price is $60, 2% exercise after exactly 6 years when the stock price is $65, and so on. Then 1% of the securities owned by an investor will provide a $20 payoff after 5 years, 2% will provide a payoff of $25 after 6 years, and so on.

Zions Bancorp tested the idea using its own stock option grant to its employees. It sold the securities using a Dutch auction process. In this individuals or companies can submit a bid indicating the price they are prepared to pay and the number of options they are prepared to buy. The clearing price is the highest bid such that the aggregate number of options sought at that price or a higher price equals or exceeds the number of options for sale. Buyers who have bid more than the clearing price get their orders filled at the clearing price and the buyer who bid the clearing price gets the remainder. Zions Bancorp announced that it had received SEC approval for its market-based approach in October 2007, but the approach has not been used to any great extent.

Definition: A systematic risk is one that influences a large number of assets, each to a greater or lesser extent. Because systematic risks have marketwide effects, they are sometimes called market risks. 
 An unsystematic risk is one that affects a single asset or a small group of assets. Because these risks are unique to individual companies or assets, they are sometimes called unique or asset-specific risks. We will use these terms interchangeably. 

 The distinction between a systematic risk and an unsystematic risk is never really as exact as we make it out to be. Even the most narrow and peculiar bit of news about a company ripples through the economy. This is true because every enterprise, no matter how tiny, is a part of the economy. It's like the tale of a kingdom that was lost because one horse lost a shoe. This is mostly hairsplitting, however. Some risks are clearly much more general than others. We'll see some evidence on this point in just a moment.

The distinction between the types of risk allows us to break down the surprise portion, \(U\), of the return on the Flyers stock into two parts. Earlier, we had the actual return broken down into its expected and surprise components:

\[R = \text{E}(R) + U\]

We now recognize that the total surprise component for Flyers, \(U\), has a systematic and an unsystematic component, so:

\[R = \text{E}(R) + \text{Systematic portion} + \text{Unsystematic portion}\]

Because it is traditional, we will use the Greek letter epsilon, **e**, to stand for the unsystematic portion. Because systematic risks are often called market risks, we will use the letter \(m\) to stand for the systematic part of the surprise. With these symbols, we can rewrite the formula for the total return:

\[R = \text{E}(R) + U=E(R)+m+\epsilon\]

The important thing about the way we have broken down the total surprise, \(U\), is that the unsystematic portion, **e**, is more or less unique to Flyers. For this reason, it is unrelated to the unsystematic portion of return on most other assets. To see why this is important, we need to return to the subject of portfolio risk.

Finance term: non-dividend-paying stock,Binomial tree
Definition: The binomial tree valuation approach divides the life of an option into small time intervals of length \(\Delta t\), where the price of the underlying asset can move to one of two values, \(Su\) or \(Sd\). Here, \(u > 1\) indicates an "up" movement and \(d < 1\) a "down" movement. The probability of an up movement is denoted by \(p\), while the probability of a down movement is \(1-p\).

### Risk-Neutral Valuation

The risk-neutral valuation principle allows for the valuation of derivatives under the assumption that expected returns from all traded assets equal the risk-free interest rate. This involves the following steps:

1. Assume the expected return from all assets is the risk-free interest rate, \(r\).
2. Value derivative payoffs by calculating their expected values and discounting them at the risk-free rate.

### Determination of \(p\), \(u\), and \(d\)

To maintain correct mean and variance for asset price changes during the interval \(\Delta t\), the expected return from the asset, taking into account its yield \(q\), is \(r - q\). Hence, the expected asset price at time \(\Delta t\) is given by:

\[
Se^{(r-q)\Delta t} = pSu + (1-p)Sd
\]

This simplifies to:

\[
e^{(r-q)\Delta t} = pu + (1-p)d \tag{21.1}
\]

The variance of the variable \(R\) (percentage change in asset price) becomes:

\[
pu^{2} + (1-p)d^{2} - e^{2(r-q)\Delta t}
\]

Since variance is unaffected by constants, we have \(\sigma^{2}\Delta t\) as the variance of \(R\):

\[
pu^{2} + (1-p)d^{2} - e^{2(r-q)\Delta t} = \sigma^{2}\Delta t
\]

From these, employing \(u = 1/d\) leads to the equations:

\[
e^{(r-q)\Delta t}(u + d) - ud - e^{2(r-q)\Delta t} = \sigma^{2}\Delta t \tag{21.2}
\]

A solution yields:

\[
p = \frac{a - d}{u - d} \tag{21.4}
\]
\[
u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}} \tag{21.5}
\]
\[
d = e^{-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}} \tag{21.6}
\]
\[
a = e^{(r - q)\Delta t} \tag{21.7}
\]

### Tree of Asset Prices

At time \(0\), the asset price \(S_0\) is known. The binomial model generates a price tree, with possible prices at each node calculated as:

\[
S_{0}u^{j}d^{i-j}, \quad j=0, 1, \ldots, i
\]

The tree structure ensures recombination, meaning a path that results in the same price can come from different up and down movements.

### Working Backward through the Tree

The option valuation starts at expiration (time \(T\)), where a call option is valued as \(\max(S_{T} - K, 0)\) and a put option as \(\max(K - S_{T}, 0)\). The value of the option at prior nodes is determined by risk-neutral expectations.

For an American option, early exercise potential is checked:

For a call:

\[
f_{i,j} = \max\{S_{0}u^{j}d^{i-j} - K, e^{-r\Delta t}[pf_{i+1,j+1} + (1-p)f_{i+1,j}]\}
\]

For a put:

\[
f_{i,j} = \max\{K - S_{0}u^{j}d^{i-j}, e^{-r\Delta t}[pf_{i+1,j+1} + (1-p)f_{i+1,j}]\}
\]

### Estimating Delta and Other Greek Letters

Delta (\(\Delta\)) is calculated as:

\[
\Delta = \frac{f_{1,1} - f_{1,0}}{S_{0}u - S_{0}d} \tag{21.8}
\]

Gamma (\(\Gamma\)) and theta (\(\Theta\)) can also be derived through respective changes in values across time steps. Vega (\(\mathcal{V}\)) and rho can be estimated similarly.

Finance term: side effects,Incremental cash flows
Definition: Remember that the incremental cash flows for a project include all the resulting changes in the _firm's_ future cash flows. It would not be unusual for a project to have side, or spillover, effects, both good and bad. For example, in 2005, the time between the theatrical release of a feature film and the release of the DVD had shrunk to 137 days compared to 200 days in 1998. This shortened release time was blamed for at least part of the decline in movie theater box office receipts. Of course, retailers cheered the move because it was credited with increasing DVD sales. A negative impact on the cash flows of an existing product from the introduction of a new product is called **erosion**.3 In this case, the cash flows from the new line should be adjusted downward to reflect lost profits on other lines.

Footnote 3: More colorfully, erosion is sometimes called _piracy_ or _cannibalism_.

In accounting for erosion, it is important to recognize that any sales lost as a result of launching a new product might be lost anyway because of future competition. Erosion is relevant only when the sales would not otherwise be lost.

Side effects show up in a lot of different ways. For example, one of Walt Disney Company's concerns when it built Euro Disney was that the new park would drain visitors from the Florida park, a popular vacation destination for Europeans.

There are beneficial spillover effects, of course. For example, you might think that Hewlett-Packard would have been concerned when the price of a printer that sold for $500 to $600 in 1994 declined to below $100 by 2007, but such was not the case. HP realized that the big money is in the consumables that printer owners buy to keep their printers going, such as ink-jet cartridges, laser toner cartridges, and special paper. The profit margins for these products are substantial.

Definition: The volatility smile is a crucial concept in pricing foreign currency options, characterized by lower implied volatility for at-the-money options and higher volatility for options moving into or out of the money. The volatility smile depicted in Figure 20.1 relates to the implied distribution shown in Figure 20.2, which reveals that the implied distribution has heavier tails compared to a lognormal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation. This phenomenon is referred to as _kurtosis_, which indicates that both extreme small and large movements in exchange rates are more likely under the implied distribution than under the lognormal distribution, while intermediate movements are less probable.

To analyze the relationship between the volatility smile and the implied distribution, consider a deep-out-of-the-money call option with a strike price of \( K_{2} \). Finance term: risk and return,Futures contract
Definition: A speculator takes a long position in a futures contract lasting for \\(T\\) years, aiming for the spot price of the asset to exceed the futures price at contract expiration. Ignoring daily settlement, the futures contract is treated like a forward contract. The speculator invests the present value of the futures price in a risk-free investment, using the proceeds to buy the asset upon maturity. The cash flows for the speculator are outlined as follows:

Today: \(-F_{0}e^{-rT}\)

End of futures contract: \(+S_{T}\)

where \\(F_{0}\\) is the current futures price, \\(S_{T}\\) is the asset price at time \\(T\\), and \\(r\\) represents the risk-free return over time \\(T\\).

To value this investment, the appropriate discount rate for the expected cash flow at time \\(T\\) equals an investor's required return, denoted as \\(k\\). The present value of the investment can thus be expressed as:

\[-F_{0}e^{-rT}+E(S_{T})e^{-kT}\\]

Assuming all investments are priced with zero net present value leads to the equation:

\[-F_{0}e^{-rT}+E(S_{T})e^{-kT}=0\\]

which simplifies to:

\[F_{0}=E(S_{T})e^{(r-k)T} \\tag{5.20}\\]

The required returns on investments depend on their systematic risk. For an investment in the asset underlying the futures contract, if returns are uncorrelated with the stock market, then \\(k=r\\), resulting in:

\[F_{0}=E(S_{T})\\]

This demonstrates that the futures price serves as an unbiased estimate of the expected future spot price under these conditions.

Conversely, if the asset's return is positively correlated with the stock market, then \\(k>r\\). This indicates that:

\[F_{0}<E(S_{T})\\]

Thus, when the asset has positive systematic risk, the futures price likely understates the expected future spot price. A typical example of this scenario is a stock index, where returns generally surpass the risk-free rate, \\(r\\), factoring in dividends that yield \\(q\\), leading to an increase in the index greater than \\(r-q\\).

In the case of negative correlation with the stock market, where \\(k<r\\), it yields:

\[F_{0}>E(S_{T})\\]

This implies that with negative systematic risk, the futures price tends to overstate the expected future spot price. 

These results are concisely summarized, illustrating the relationship between futures prices, expected spot price, and systematic risk within the financial market context.
\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Relationship between futures price and expected future spot price.}
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
\textbf{Underlying asset} & \textbf{Relationship of expected return k from asset to risk-free rate r} & \textbf{Relationship of futures price F to expected future spot price E($S_T$)} \\ \hline
No systematic risk & $k = r$ & $F_0 = E(S_T)$ \\ \hline
Positive systematic risk & $k > r$ & $F_0 < E(S_T)$ \\ \hline
Negative systematic risk & $k < r$ & $F_0 > E(S_T)$ \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

data.content:
Finance term: Speculative Motive,Keynes's Liquidity Preference Theory
Definition: If Keynes had ended his theory with the transactions and precautionary motives, income would be the only important determinant of the demand for money, and he would not have added much to the classical approach. However, Keynes took the view that people also hold money as a store of wealth. He called this reason for holding money the speculative motive. Because he believed that wealth is tied closely to income, the speculative component of money demand would be related to income. However, Keynes looked more carefully at other factors that influence the decisions regarding how much money to hold as a store of wealth, especially interest rates.
Keynes divided the assets that can be used to store wealth into two categories: money and bonds. He then asked the following question: Why would individuals decide to hold their wealth in the form of money rather than bonds?
Thinking back to the discussion of the theory of asset demand (Chapter 5), you would want to hold money if its expected return was greater than the expected return from holding bonds. Keynes assumed that the expected return on money was zero because in his time, unlike today, most checkable deposits did not earn interest. For bonds, there are two components of the expected return: the interest payment and the _expected_ rate of capital gains.
You learned in Chapter 4 that when interest rates rise, the price of a bond falls. If you expect interest rates to rise, you expect the price of the bond to fall and therefore expect to suffer a negative capital gain--that is, a capital loss. If you expect the rise in interest rates to be substantial enough, the capital loss might outweigh the interest payment, and your _expected_ return on the bond would be negative. In this case, you would want to store your wealth as money because its expected return is higher; its zero return exceeds the negative return on the bond.
Keynes assumed that individuals believe that interest rates gravitate to some normal value (an assumption less plausible in today's world). If interest rates are below this normal value, individuals expect the interest rate on bonds to rise in the future and so expect to suffer capital losses on them. As a result, individuals will be more likely to hold their wealth as money rather than bonds, and the demand for money will be high.
What would you expect to happen to the demand for money when interest rates are above the normal value? In general, people will expect interest rates to fall, bond prices to rise, and capital gains to be realized. At higher interest rates, they are more likely to expect the return from holding a bond to be positive, thus exceeding the expected return from holding money. They will be more likely to hold bonds than money, and the demand for money will be quite low. From Keynes's reasoning, we can conclude that as interest rates rise, the demand for money falls, and therefore _money demand is negatively related to the level of interest rates_.

data.content:
Finance term: role of correlation,Basket credit default swap
Definition: The cost of protection in a _k_th-to-default CDS or a tranche of a CDO is critically dependent on default correlation. Suppose that a basket of 100 reference entities is used to define a 5-year _k_th-to-default CDS and that each reference entity has a risk-neutral probability of 2% of defaulting during the 5 years. When the default correlation between the reference entities is zero the binomial distribution shows that the probability of one or more defaults during the 5 years is 86.74% and the probability of 10 or more defaults is 0.0034%. A first-to-default CDS is therefore quite valuable whereas a tenth-to-default CDS is worth almost nothing.

As the default correlation increases the probability of one or more defaults declines and the probability of 10 or more defaults increases. In the limit where the default correlation between the reference entities is perfect the probability of one or more defaults equals the probability of ten or more defaults and is 2%. This is because in this extreme situation the reference entities are essentially the same. Either they all default (with probability 2%) or none of them default (with probability 98%).

The valuation of a tranche of a synthetic CDO is similarly dependent on default correlation. If the correlation is low, the junior equity tranche is very risky and the senior tranches are very safe. As the default correlation increases, the junior tranches become less risky and the senior tranches become more risky. In the limit where the default correlation is perfect and the recovery rate is zero, the tranches are equally risky.

While a positive estimated NPV can suggest a good investment, conflicting signals such as a long payback period and low Average Accounting Return (AAR) necessitate caution. Capital expenditures by corporations are substantial; for example, ExxonMobil planned to increase its capital spending by about 35 percent to $11 billion in 2006, Toyota aimed for $14 billion, and Shell Oil projected $21 billion for capital investments in the same year. Industry-wide, the worldwide semiconductor sector was expected to rise capital spending by 10 percent to $50.4 billion in 2006, marking the second largest total in the industry's history after 2000, when $60.3 billion was spent.

In aggregate, capital investment for the U.S. economy totaled $1.05 trillion in 2004, $975 billion in 2003, and $953 billion in 2002, nearing $3 trillion over those three years. Given these large sums, it is critical for businesses to excel in analyzing capital expenditures.

Finance term: LM Curve,Equilibrium in the Market for Money: The LM Curve,The ISLM Model
Definition: The LM curve represents the combinations of interest rates and aggregate output in which the quantity of money demanded equals the quantity of money supplied. In Keynesian economics, the equilibrium level of interest rates is determined by the market for money, where the quantity of money demanded matches the quantity of money supplied.

The LM curve is derived while keeping the real money supply fixed at the level of \(\overline{M}/P\). Each aggregate output level yields its own money demand curve, reflecting changes in transaction levels in the economy, which affect money demand. For instance, at aggregate output \(Y_{1}\), the money demand curve is represented as \(M^{d}(Y_{1})\). This curve slopes downward; lower interest rates reduce the opportunity cost of holding money, increasing the quantity of money demanded.

As output increases to \(Y_{2}\), the money demand curve shifts rightward to \(M^{d}(Y_{2})\), reflecting higher money demand at any given interest rate. Equilibrium occurs at a higher interest rate \(i_{2}\) compared to \(i_{1}\) with \(Y_{1}\). A further increase to \(Y_{3}\) results in an even higher equilibrium interest rate \(i_{3}\). These equilibria are summarized in panel (b), where interest rates corresponding to different output levels are plotted, forming the LM curve. The positive slope of the LM curve derives from the relationship that rising output increases money demand and, consequently, the equilibrium interest rate.

The LM curve delineates points satisfying the equilibrium condition where money demanded equals money supplied. It indicates the necessary interest rate for each level of aggregate output to achieve equilibrium in the money market. When aggregate output rises, money demand increases and leads to higher interest rates, maintaining equilibrium.

If the economy operates to the left of the LM curve, it indicates excess money supply. For example, at point A, with an interest rate \(i_{3}\) and aggregate output \(Y_{1}\), the rate is above the equilibrium level, resulting in individuals holding more money than desired. To rectify this imbalance, they will purchase bonds, driving up bond prices and reducing interest rates until equilibrium on the LM curve is reached.

Conversely, if the economy is to the right of the LM curve, there is excess demand for money. For example, at point B, with interest rate \(i_{1}\) below equilibrium, individuals desire to hold more money than currently available. To obtain additional money, they will sell bonds, reducing bond prices and raising the interest rate until it aligns with an equilibrium point on the LM curve. 

In summary, the LM curve provides a framework for understanding the relationship between interest rates and aggregate output in the context of money supply and demand equilibrium within an economy.

The average of the bid-offer rate being exchanged for six-month LIBOR in swaps of all maturities is currently 5% per annum with continuous compounding.What is the current value of the swap to the party paying floating? (Unit: dollar)

data.content:
Finance term: valuation,Interest rate swap
Definition: Interest rate swaps are financial agreements that initially have a value close to zero, but over time can attain positive or negative values. When valuing these swaps, two primary approaches can be employed using LIBOR or OIS rates as discount rates. The first approach views the swap as the difference between two bonds, while the second considers it as a portfolio of forward rate agreements (FRAs).

### Valuation in Terms of Bond Prices

Principal payments in an interest rate swap are not exchanged, but for valuation purposes, they can be assumed to be paid and received at the end of the swap term without altering its value. From the floating-rate payer's perspective, a swap is represented as a long position in a fixed-rate bond and a short position in a floating-rate bond, expressed mathematically as:

\[
V_{\text{swap}} = B_{\text{fix}} - B_{\text{fl}}
\]

where \(V_{\text{swap}}\) is the value of the swap, \(B_{\text{fl}}\) is the value of the floating-rate bond, and \(B_{\text{fix}}\) is the value of the fixed-rate bond. Conversely, for the fixed-rate payer, this relationship is:

\[
V_{\text{swap}} = B_{\text{fl}} - B_{\text{fix}}
\]

The value of the fixed-rate bond, \(B_{\text{fix}}\), is calculated using established methodologies. For the floating-rate bond, it is valued at the notional principal immediately after a payment, as it represents a "fair deal" where the borrower pays LIBOR for subsequent accrual periods. 

If the notional principal is \(L\), with the next payment occurring at time \(t^{*}\) and the floating payment determined at the last payment date as \(k^{*}\), immediately after the payment, the value is \(B_{\text{fl}} = L\). Just before the payment, \(B_{\text{fl}} = L + k^{*}\). The floating-rate bond can thus be evaluated as providing a sole cash flow of \(L + k^{*}\) at time \(t^{*}\). Its current value is given by:

\[
(L + k^{*})e^{-r^{*}t^{*}}
\]

where \(r^{*}\) signifies the LIBOR or swap zero rate for a maturity of \(t^{*}\).

### Valuation in Terms of FRAs

An interest rate swap can also be characterized as a portfolio of FRAs. For instance, a typical swap involves several semiannual payments, with the initial payments known at the swap's negotiation. Subsequent payments can be treated as FRAs. For example, payment exchanges correspond to contracts where fixed interest (e.g., at 5%) is swapped for the prevailing market 6-month rate observed at specific intervals.

Valuation of an FRA assumes realized forward interest rates, which can also be extended to valuing an interest rate swap. The process involves the following steps:

1. Calculate forward rates using the LIBOR/swap zero curve for each rate influencing swap cash flows.
2. Determine swap cash flows based on the assumption that LIBOR rates will match the calculated forward rates.
3. Discount these cash flows back using the LIBOR/swap zero curve to ascertain the swap's value.

These approaches provide robustness to the valuation of interest rate swaps, allowing clients to understand their financial positions accurately.

Finance term: Fisher effect,inflation and interest rates,Bonds
Definition: Our discussion of real and nominal returns illustrates a relationship often called the **Fisher effect** (after the great economist Irving Fisher). Because investors are ultimately concerned with what they can buy with their money, they require compensation for inflation. Let \(R\) stand for the nominal rate and \(r\) stand for the real rate. The Fisher effect tells us that the relationship between nominal rates, real rates, and inflation can be written as:

\[1 + R = (1 + r) \times (1 + h)\]

where \(h\) is the inflation rate.

In the preceding example, the nominal rate was 15.50 percent and the inflation rate was 5 percent. What was the real rate? We can determine it by plugging in these numbers:

\[1 + .1550 = (1 + r) \times (1 + .05)\]

\[1 + r = 1.1550/1.05 = 1.10\]

\[r = 10\%\]

This real rate is the same as we found before. If we take another look at the Fisher effect, we can rearrange things a little as follows:

\[1 + R = (1 + r) \times (1 + h)\]

\[R = r + h + r \times h\]

What this tells us is that the nominal rate has three components. First, there is the real rate on the investment, \(r\). Next, there is the compensation for the decrease in the value of the money originally invested because of inflation, \(h\). The third component represents compensation for the fact that the dollars earned on the investment are also worth less because of the inflation.

This third component is usually small, so it is often dropped. The nominal rate is then approximately equal to the real rate plus the inflation rate:

\[R = r + h\]

Finance term: option on a non-dividend-paying stock,American option
Definition: American call options on non-dividend-paying stocks should not be exercised before expiration. For instance, with a stock price of S70 and a strike price of S40, it is more beneficial for the investor to hold the option and exercise it at expiration. By not exercising early, the investor can earn interest on the strike price for the duration remaining until expiration and maintain the potential upside of the stock price, which could even decrease below the strike price. If an investor believes the stock is overvalued, selling the option can yield better returns since the price will exceed its intrinsic value, which is S30 in this case.

Mathematically, for an American call option, the following holds:

\[
C \geqslant S_{0} - K e^{-rT}
\]
Since \(C \geqslant c\) (where \(C\) is the American call price and \(c\) is the European call price), it follows that:

\[
C \geqslant S_{0} - K e^{-rT}
\]

Given \(r > 0\) and \(T > 0\), \(C > S_{0} - K\), implying that \(C\) is always greater than the intrinsic value prior to expiration. Hence, early exercise is never optimal, as exercising would result in \(C\) equaling the option's intrinsic value.

The two primary reasons against early exercise are the insurance aspect of the call option—protecting against stock price declines by holding the option—and the time value of money, favoring later payout of the strike price.

For American put options on non-dividend-paying stocks, early exercise can be optimal, particularly when deep in the money. For instance, if the stock price is nearly zero and the strike price is $10, exercising immediately yields $10. If delayed, the realizable gain could be less than $10. Thus, early exercise becomes more attractive as \(S_{0}\) decreases, \(r\) increases, and volatility decreases.

The bounds for European put options are defined as:

\[
\max(Ke^{-rT} - S_{0}, 0) \leqslant p \leqslant K e^{-rT}
\]

For American put options, the relationship is expressed as:

\[
P \geqslant \max(K - S_{0}, 0)
\]

This ensures that the American put price satisfies:

\[
\max(K - S_{0}, 0) \leqslant P \leqslant K
\]

When \(r > 0\), early exercise is optimal when the stock price is sufficiently low, aligning with the intrinsic value \(K - S_{0}\). The curves illustrating put option prices indicate that an American put is often worth more than a European put, due to the potential for early exercise. Consequently, the curve representing the European put price lies below that of the American put price, showing that at some points the value of the European puts is less than their intrinsic value, maintaining the relationship:

\[
P_{\text{European}} < P_{\text{American}}
\]

The dynamics of both call and put options highlight the strategies surrounding their exercise based on dividend policies, stock prices, and time to expiration.

Finance term: Stack and roll
Definition: The process of managing hedge expiration dates involves rolling forward futures contracts when the hedge expiration surpasses the delivery dates of available futures. This strategy is referred to as _stack and roll_. For example, a company employing a short hedge to mitigate the risk of selling an asset at time \(T\) can utilize several futures contracts with progressively later delivery dates.

The rolling procedure involves the following steps: 
- At time \(t_1\), short the first futures contract.
- At time \(t_2\), close out the first contract and short the second.
- This process continues until the final contract at time \(T\) is closed out.

Consider a situation where a company realizes it will have 100,000 barrels of oil to sell in June 2015 and decides to hedge with a ratio of 1.0. The current spot price is $89. Assuming only the first six delivery months have sufficient liquidity, the company shorts 100 October 2014 contracts. 

As time progresses:
- In September 2014, the hedge is rolled forward into the March 2015 contract.
- In February 2015, it is rolled forward again into the July 2015 contract.

In this example, the following outcomes occur:
- The October 2014 contract is shorted at $88.20 per barrel and closed out at $87.40, resulting in a profit of $0.80 per barrel.
- The March 2015 contract is shorted at $87.00 and closed at $86.50, yielding a profit of $0.50.
- The July 2015 contract is shorted at $86.30 and closed at $85.90, for a profit of $0.40.

The total dollar gain per barrel from the short futures contracts is calculated as follows:

\[
(88.20-87.40) + (87.00-86.50) + (86.30-85.90) = 1.70
\]

Despite this hedging strategy, oil prices drop from $89 to $86, resulting in only $1.70 per barrel compensation for a $3.00 decline in price. This outcome highlights that total compensation for a decline is not always realized when futures prices are below spot prices; the goal is to lock in a reasonable futures price corresponding to June 2015 if actively traded.

In practical scenarios, companies generally face ongoing exposure to their underlying asset and use 1-month futures contracts due to their liquidity. They initially stack contracts to cover their exposure until the end of the hedging horizon. After one month, they close all contracts and roll them into new 1-month contracts to address their evolving exposure.

A notable case is that of Metallgesellschaft, a German company in the early 1990s, which faced difficulties using this strategy. As the prices of commodities fell, it incurred immediate cash outflows from futures while awaiting gains from contracts, leading to liquidity issues due to mismatched cash flows between hedge timing and the asset position being hedged. Such potential liquidity problems must be carefully considered when planning a hedging strategy.

The process of managing hedge expiration dates involves rolling forward futures contracts when the hedge expiration surpasses the delivery dates of available futures. This strategy is referred to as _stack and roll_. For example, a company employing a short hedge to mitigate the risk of selling an asset at time \(T\) can utilize several futures contracts with progressively later delivery dates.

The rolling procedure involves the following steps: 
- At time \(t_1\), short the first futures contract.
- At time \(t_2\), close out the first contract and short the second.
- This process continues until the final contract at time \(T\) is closed out.

Consider a situation where a company realizes it will have 100,000 barrels of oil to sell in June 2015 and decides to hedge with a ratio of 1.0. The current spot price is $89. Assuming only the first six delivery months have sufficient liquidity, the company shorts 100 October 2014 contracts. 

As time progresses:
- In September 2014, the hedge is rolled forward into the March 2015 contract.
- In February 2015, it is rolled forward again into the July 2015 contract.

- The October 2014 contract is shorted at $88.20 per barrel and closed out at $87.40, resulting in a profit of $0.80 per barrel.

\[

\]

Finance term: Conversion factor
Definition: The Treasury bond futures contract allows the short position holder to deliver any bond maturing between 15 and 25 years. The price received for the delivered bond is determined by a parameter known as the _conversion factor_, calculated based on the bond's value and the most recent settlement price of the futures contract. The price received, taking into account accrued interest, can be represented as:

\[
\text{(Most recent settlement price} \times \text{Conversion factor)} + \text{Accrued interest}
\]

Each contract corresponds to $100,000 face value of bonds. For example, if the most recent settlement price is 90-00, the conversion factor is 1.3800, and the accrued interest is $3 per $100 face value, the cash received by the short position holder is given by:

\[
(1.3800 \times 90.00) + 3.00 = \$127.20
\]

Thus, for a contract, the short position holder delivers $100,000 worth of bonds and receives $127,200.

The conversion factor is determined based on the assumption that the interest rate for all maturities is 6% per annum (with semiannual compounding). Maturity and payment dates are rounded down to the nearest three months. If the rounding results in an exact number of 6-month periods, the first coupon is assumed to be paid in 6 months. If it has an extra three months, the first coupon is assumed to be paid after 3 months, from which accrued interest is deducted.

For example, a 10% coupon bond with 20 years and 2 months to maturity is simplified to a bond with 20 years to maturity for conversion factor calculation. The first coupon payment is assumed after 6 months, and with a semiannual discount rate of 3%, the value of the bond is:

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{40} \frac{5}{1.03^{i}} + \frac{100}{1.03^{40}} = \$146.23
\]

Dividing by the face value of $100 gives a conversion factor of 1.4623.

In another example, an 8% coupon bond with 18 years and 4 months to maturity is treated as having 18 years and 3 months. The payment values are discounted at the semiannual rate of 3%:

\[
4 + \sum_{i=1}^{36} \frac{4}{1.03^{i}} + \frac{100}{1.03^{36}} = \$125.83
\]

The 3-month interest rate is calculated as:

\[
\sqrt{1.03} - 1 \text{ or } 1.4889\%
\]

Thus, further discounting gives:

\[
\frac{125.83}{1.014889} = \$123.99
\]

After subtracting accrued interest of $2.00, the final value becomes $121.99, resulting in a conversion factor of 1.2199.

Finance term: OIS discounting
Definition: LIBOR-for-fixed swaps can be valued by assuming realized forward LIBOR rates. When transacted at mid-market swap rates, these swaps are worth zero, providing a means to deduce LIBOR forward rates. Notably, LIBOR forward rates derived through overnight indexed swap (OIS) discounting differ from those obtained via LIBOR discounting.

In **Example 9.2**, if the 1-year LIBOR rate is 5% and the 2-year LIBOR-for-fixed swap rate is 6% with annual payments, a bank using LIBOR rates for discounting can determine the zero rate \(R\) by solving the equation:

\[
\frac{6}{1.05} + \frac{106}{(1+R)^{2}} = 100
\]

This yields \(R = 6.030\%\). The forward LIBOR rate \(F\) for the 1-year period beginning in year 1 can then be calculated as:

\[
F = \frac{1.06030^{2}}{1.05} - 1 = 7.0707\%
\]

To verify, setting the swap's value to zero leads to:

\[
\frac{1}{1.05} + \frac{6 - 100F}{1.06030^{2}} = 0
\]

Solving for \(F\) again results in \(F = 7.0707\%\).

**Example 9.3** presents a similar setup with OIS discounting. With the same LIBOR rates but OIS zero rates at 4.5% and 5.5%, the equation becomes:

\[
\frac{1}{1.045} + \frac{6 - 100F}{1.055^{2}} = 0
\]

Solving gives \(F = 7.0651\%\). Transitioning from LIBOR to OIS discounting results in a mere reduction in the forward LIBOR rate from 7.0707% to 7.0651%.

These examples illustrate how a forward LIBOR curve can be constructed using OIS rates as risk-free discount rates. Swaps with different payment intervals, such as every 3 or 6 months, enable the calculation of corresponding forward rates. Interpolation aids in creating complete forward LIBOR curves.

When utilizing OIS discounting for swaps, cash flows are determined using corresponding forward LIBOR rates derived from calculated forward LIBOR curves, which are then discounted at the appropriate OIS zero rates.

In the context of caps, floors, and swaptions, when OIS discounting is employed, the forward LIBOR rate between times \(t_k\) and \(t_{k+1}\) is denoted as \(E_{k+1}(R_{k})\), with \(R_{k}\) being the realized LIBOR rate for that period, and \(E_{k+1}\) representing expectations in a forward risk-neutral world.

The equations for valuation of caps and swaptions remain valid with OIS discounting: for caps, equation (29.9) holds true, leading to (29.7) with:

\[
F_{k} = E_{k+1}(R_{k}) \quad \text{and} \quad P(0,t_{k+1}) \text{ from the OIS zero curve.}
\]

For swaptions, the annuity factor \(A\) is calculated from the OIS zero curve, and the forward swap rate \(s_{0}\) is computed from forward LIBOR rates, ensuring the forward swap is valued at zero under OIS discounting.

Finance term: historical simulation,Value at risk (VaR)
Definition: Historical simulation is one popular way of estimating VaR. It involves using past data as a guide to what will happen in the future. Suppose that we want to calculate VaR for a portfolio using a one-day time horizon, a 99% confidence level, and 501 days of data. (The time horizon and confidence level are those typically used for a market risk VaR calculation; 501 is a popular choice for the number of days of data used because, as we shall see, it leads to 500 scenarios being created.) The first step is to identify the market variables affecting the portfolio. These will typically be interest rates, equity prices, commodity prices, and so on. All prices are measured in the domestic currency. For example, one market variable for a German bank is likely to be the S&P 500 measured in euros.

Data are collected on movements in the market variables over the most recent 501 days. This provides 500 alternative scenarios for what can happen between today and tomorrow. Denote the first day for which we have data as Day 0, the second day as Day 1, and so on. Scenario 1 is where the percentage changes in the values of all variables are the same as they were between Day 0 and Day 1, Scenario 2 is where they are the same as between Day 1 and Day 2, and so on. For each scenario, the dollar change in the value of the portfolio between today and tomorrow is calculated. This defines a probability distribution for daily loss (gains are negative losses) in the value of our portfolio. The 99th percentile of the distribution can be estimated as the fifth-highest loss.2 The estimate of VaR is the loss when we are at this 99th percentile point. We are 99% certain that we will not take a loss greater than the VaR estimate if the changes in market variables in the last 501 days are representative of what will happen between today and tomorrow.

To express the approach algebraically, define \(v_{i}\) as the value of a market variable on Day \(i\) and suppose that today is Day \(n\). The \(i\)th scenario in the historical simulation approach assumes that the value of the market variable tomorrow will be

\[\text{Value under }i\text{th scenario}=v_{n}\,\frac{v_{i}}{v_{i-1}}\]
